---
title: "Coding exercises: getting started"
---

The lectures describe algorithms in **pseudocode**: plain steps, close to the math, that you can
follow without knowing any programming language. To write the algorithms yourself, exercise pages
end with a section **Code**, after the pen-and-paper questions and the demo.

The coding exercises use [Rust](https://www.rust-lang.org/) and a small image library written for
this course, `imgcourse`. It is made to be **read**, not to be fast. An image is a grid of
numbers, and you change it with plain loops that look like the formulas on the slides. You do
not need to know Rust well. The exercises use only variables, loops, functions and small arrays,
and every task comes with a hint.

## 1. Install Rust

Install Rust with **rustup**, following the instructions at <https://rustup.rs>:

- on Linux and macOS, one command in a terminal;
- on Windows, an installer; it may ask you to install the Visual Studio C++ build tools first.

This gives you `cargo`, the tool that builds, runs and tests Rust programs. Check it in a new terminal:

```
cargo --version
```

A good editor is [VS Code](https://code.visualstudio.com/) with the **rust-analyzer** extension.
It shows types and errors as you type, and the documentation of a function when you hover over it.

## 2. Download the code

[**Download imageanalysis-code.zip**](downloads/imageanalysis-code.zip) (about 90 KB) and
unpack it anywhere. It is one folder, `imageanalysis-code`:

```
imageanalysis-code/
  Cargo.toml     lists the projects below (a Cargo "workspace")
  imgcourse/     the image library
  starter/       a first program
  images/        one project per unit with coding exercises
  kernels/
  fourier/
  pca/
```

Open a terminal **in that folder** and run the first program:

```
cargo run -p starter
```

The first build downloads a few packages (for reading and writing image files) and takes a
minute; later builds take seconds. The program prints the size of the course micrograph and
writes two pictures to `out/starter/`. Open them, then open `starter/src/main.rs`, read it,
change something, and run it again.

## 3. Do an exercise

Each unit's project has the same four files:

| File | What it is |
|---|---|
| `src/exercise.rs` | **your code**: functions whose body is `todo!()`, each with a description and a hint |
| `tests/check.rs` | checks, mostly the numbers of the pen-and-paper exercises |
| `src/main.rs` | runs your functions on real images and writes pictures to `out/<unit>/` |
| `src/solution.rs` | a model solution; look at it after you have tried |

For example, for the filtering unit:

```
cargo test -p kernels                      # check your code: every todo!() fails until you write it
cargo run -p kernels                       # run your code on the micrograph, pictures in out/kernels/
cargo test -p kernels --features solution  # the same checks on the model solution
cargo run -p kernels --features solution   # the model solution's pictures
```

A failing check prints what it expected and what your code gave, for example
`row 3, column 2: got 2.5, expected 3`. Work through the functions in order, C1, C2, …; each
check is named after the function it tests.

## 4. The library on one page

```rust
use imgcourse::*;

let img = samples::cell();              // the course micrograph, 256 × 256, values 0..1
let img = load_gray("my-image.png");    // or any PNG, JPEG or TIFF file, as grey values 0..1

img.width(); img.height();              // the size
img[(x, y)]                             // pixel at column x, row y (both from 0)
out[(x, y)] = 0.5;                      // set a pixel (out must be `let mut out = ...`)
img.get_border(x, y, Border::Clamp)     // x, y may lie outside: Zero, Clamp, Mirror or Wrap

let mut out = Image::new(w, h, 0.0);    // a new w × h image filled with 0
for (x, y) in img.coords() { ... }      // every pixel position, row by row
img.map(|v| 1.0 - v)                    // a new image: the same function on every value
img.map_xy(|x, y, v| ...)               // ... that can also use the position
a.zip_map(&b, |p, q| p - q)             // combine two images pixel by pixel
img.crop(x0, y0, w, h)                  // a piece of the image
img.min(); img.max(); img.mean();       // for images of f32
Image::from_rows(&[[1., 2.], [3., 4.]]) // a small image written out by hand
println!("{img:.2}");                   // print a small image as a table, 2 decimals

save_gray(&img, "out/a.png");           // 0 = black, 1 = white
save_gray_stretched(&img, "out/b.png"); // smallest value black, largest white
save_gray_signed(&img, "out/c.png");    // 0 = grey: for edge filters with negative values

Complex::new(re, im)                    // complex numbers for Fourier: + - * work
Complex::from_angle(theta)              // e^{iθ}
let mut rng = Rng::new(seed);           // random numbers: rng.uniform(), rng.normal()
```

Three conventions to remember:

- **Positions.** `(x, y)` is column `x` from the left and row `y` from the top, counted from 0.
  The pen-and-paper exercises count rows and columns from 1, so "row 3, column 2" is `(1, 2)`.
- **Values.** Grey values are `f32` between 0 (black) and 1 (white). An 8-bit file is divided by
  255 when it is read, and a 16-bit file by 65535.
- **Angles.** Because `y` points down, a rotation by a positive angle turns the image
  **clockwise** on the screen.

The full documentation of the library, with examples, opens in your browser with
`cargo doc -p imgcourse --open`.

## 5. Your own project

To use the library in a project of your own, put the project folder next to `imgcourse/` (for
example in `imageanalysis-code/`). A minimal `Cargo.toml`:

```toml
[package]
name = "myproject"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2021"

[dependencies]
imgcourse = { path = "../imgcourse" }
```

and `src/main.rs`:

```rust
use imgcourse::*;

fn main() {
    let img = samples::cell();
    let out = img.map(|v| if v > 0.5 { 1.0 } else { 0.0 });
    save_gray(&out, "out/threshold.png");
}
```

Run it with `cargo run` in the project folder. If the project lives inside `imageanalysis-code`,
also add its name to `members` in `imageanalysis-code/Cargo.toml`; then `cargo run -p myproject`
works from there too.

## Just enough Rust

The exercises need only a handful of constructs; the hints show the rest.

```rust
let n = 5;                       // a variable; it cannot change ...
let mut sum = 0.0;               // ... unless it is declared mut
for i in 0..n { sum += 1.0; }    // a loop over 0, 1, ..., n − 1
for d in -1..=1isize { }         // -1, 0, 1 (with ..= the end is included)
let x = 3usize;                  // whole numbers for positions: usize (never negative) ...
let left = x as isize - 1;       // ... and isize, which may be negative; convert with `as`
let v = x as f32 * 0.5;          // f32: a decimal number
let k = [[1.0, 2.0], [3.0, 4.0]];  k[1][0]   // fixed-size arrays: row 1, column 0 is 3.0
let mut list = Vec::new(); list.push(2.5);   // a list that grows
let square = |v: f32| v * v;     // a small function without a name (a closure), for map
fn twice(v: f32) -> f32 { 2.0 * v }          // a function; the last line is its result
```

For more, the free book [The Rust Programming Language](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/),
chapters 1 to 3, covers everything used here.

## Units with coding exercises

- [Images as arrays & geometric transforms](images/exercise.qmd#code): interpolation, homogeneous coordinates, warping an image.
- [Filtering & convolution](kernels/exercise.qmd#code): 3 × 3 filters, border rules, the gradient, separable filters.
- [Images in frequency space](fourier/exercise.qmd#code): the DFT from its definition, frequency responses, low-pass filtering.
- [Principal component analysis](pca/exercise.qmd#code): covariance, eigenvectors, projection, principal components of image patches.
